finicky

FIN-ih-kee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Finicky is very picky about one's needs.

The finicky toddler refused to eat anything that touched another food on his plate.

Worked Example

Their cat was so finicky about food that she would sniff, then abandon, three different brands in one sitting.

Finicky describes someone -- often about food or personal comfort -- who is hard to satisfy because of narrow, particular preferences.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

picky: Picky is the plain, everyday word for being hard to please. Finicky turns the pickiness up a notch and makes it fussier: a finicky eater doesn't just have favorites -- they reject food over tiny details, like how it was cut or which bowl it came in.

choosy: Choosy means selective in a mild, sensible way: you know what you like and you pick accordingly, without drama. Finicky is choosiness gone overboard -- an itch about small details that makes someone genuinely hard to satisfy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

adaptable: easily satisfied with different options

easygoing: not fussy about small preferences

Where it sits · how demanding the pickiness gets — selective → finicky → compulsive

selective vs. finicky: Being selective just means you have clear preferences and choose with care; finicky goes further, fussing over tiny details most people would never even notice.

compulsive vs. finicky: Compulsive pickiness goes a step beyond finicky: a finicky eater fusses over small preferences, while a compulsive one is driven by a need too strong to resist.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Finicky's exact origin is uncertain -- some sources link it loosely to the older word "fine," but no confirmed root survives elsewhere in common English.

Use the root in a new word: finical

Use the root in a new word: finical: "Finical," an older and now rare relative of finicky, was used in the 1600s to describe someone excessively dainty or fussy.
